title: How a Chemical Stopped Napoleon From Conquering Russia
description:
What if one of history’s greatest generals was defeated not just by men, but by chemistry? In this video, we uncover the story of how Napoleon Bonaparte’s Russian campaign of 1812 may have been undone by an element as simple as tin.

Napoleon’s army of over half a million marched into the Russian winter, facing brutal sub-zero temperatures. Their uniforms were fastened with shiny tin buttons — but tin has a hidden property called allotropy. At low temperatures, beta-tin can transform into alpha-tin in a process known as tin pest, crumbling into dust. Exposed to the Russian cold, the buttons may have disintegrated, leaving soldiers unable to close their coats and vulnerable to the deadly freeze.

We explain what allotropy is, with familiar examples like diamond, graphite, and coal, and why the same element can exist in radically different forms. We also examine how much of this story is fact versus legend, and how disease, starvation, and harsh weather also contributed to Napoleon’s defeat.

If you’ve searched for “Napoleon Russia campaign,” “tin pest explained,” “allotropy chemistry example,” “Napoleon defeat science,” “how cold destroyed Napoleon’s army,” or “tin buttons Napoleon myth”, this video shows how history and science collide to tell a fascinating tale. Don’t forget to like, share, and subscribe for more stories where chemistry changed history.
